item.ptxt: During air-fuel ratio feedback, if the air fuel ratio sensor continues to output lean even though the oxygen sensor is outputting rich, the engine control computer sets DTC P2195/21 and illuminates the check engine warning light.

Also, during air-fuel ratio feedback, if the air fuel ratio sensor continues to output rich even though the oxygen sensor is outputting lean, the engine control computer sets DTC P2196/21 and illuminates the check engine warning light.

When the air fuel ratio sensor current during fuel cut is approximately 3.6 mA or more (in this case P2195/21) or approximately 1.0 mA or less (in this case P2196/21), the engine control computer sets a DTC and illuminates the check engine warning light.

item.ptxt: If the air fuel ratio sensor output voltage remains at approximately 3.3 V in any of the conditions, including the above condition (see the malfunction case in the illustration), the air fuel ratio sensor may have an open circuit. (This also occurs when the air fuel ratio sensor heater has an open circuit.)
If the air fuel ratio sensor output voltage remains at approximately 3.8 V or more, or 2.8 V or less in any of the conditions, the air fuel ratio sensor may have a short circuit.
The engine control computer stops fuel injection during engine deceleration (fuel cut). This causes a lean condition and results in a momentary increase in the air fuel ratio sensor output voltage.
While driving:

During fuel enrichment, the air fuel ratio sensor output voltage may be below 2.8 V. For the vehicle, this corresponds to sudden acceleration with the accelerator pedal fully depressed, such as when overtaking. The air fuel ratio sensor is functioning normally.

The air fuel ratio sensor is a current output element. Therefore, the current is converted into voltage inside the engine control computer. Measuring the voltage at the air fuel ratio sensor connector or engine control computer connector will show a constant voltage result.
